items.prompt: Read this function. Explain what it does, its time complexity, and anything you'd flag in review.

fault_label.description: `seen` is a list, so `in seen` is an O(n) scan inside the loop -> O(n^2) overall, though it mimics the O(n) hash-set two-sum idiom.

expected_observations.statement: Returns True iff two elements of nums sum to target.
Real time complexity is O(n^2) because membership test on a list is O(n); it only looks like the O(n) set idiom.
Fix: use a set for `seen` to get O(1) membership and O(n) overall.
Space is O(n); returning True on the first matching pair is correct.
Handles empty input and the x+x same-value pairing correctly.

decoys.why_it_looks_wrong: The early `return True` looks like it could miss later pairs.
decoys.why_its_actually_fine: Returning on the first found pair is correct — the function only needs existence, not all pairs.

items.prompt: Read this function. Explain its behaviour across repeated calls and flag any issue.

fault_label.description: Default `cart=[]` is evaluated once at definition; all default-arg calls share one list, so state persists across calls.

expected_observations.statement: Appends item to cart and returns it.
The default [] is created once at function-definition time, so calls that omit cart share and mutate the same list across calls.
Fix: default to None, then create a new list inside when cart is None.
The bug only surfaces when the caller omits cart; passing an explicit list works fine.
This is the classic mutable-default-argument pitfall.

decoys.why_it_looks_wrong: Mutating the passed-in `cart` parameter in place can look like a side-effect smell.
decoys.why_its_actually_fine: In-place append of a caller-supplied list is intended; the defect is the default value, not the append.

static_findings: mutable default argument (list literal) on add_to_cart

items.prompt: Read this search. Explain what it does and whether it is correct for all inputs.

fault_label.description: Loop condition `lo < hi` exits when lo == hi, skipping the final single-element window; a target that reduces to that window is missed. Should be `lo <= hi`.

expected_observations.statement: Binary search over a sorted array; returns the index of target or -1.
Condition `lo < hi` stops when lo == hi, so an element sitting in the final one-wide window is never checked.
Fix: use `lo <= hi`.
Concrete failing case: searching for the last element (e.g. 9 in [1,3,5,7,9]) returns -1.
Complexity is still O(log n); the defect is correctness, not performance.

decoys.why_it_looks_wrong: `mid = (lo + hi) // 2` is the famous integer-overflow binary-search bug.
decoys.why_its_actually_fine: Python ints are arbitrary-precision, so there is no overflow here — flagging it shows pattern-matching, not reasoning about this language.

static_findings: binary search loop uses strict `<` bound

check.reference:
def binary_search(arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr)-1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid=(lo+hi)//2
        if arr[mid]==target: return mid
        elif arr[mid]<target: lo=mid+1
        else: hi=mid-1
    return -1

items.prompt: This query is meant to report total order revenue. Read it and explain the result it actually produces.

artifact.schema: orders(id, customer_id, total); order_tags(order_id, tag)  -- an order can have many tags

fault_label.description: Joining orders (1) to order_tags (many) fans each order out to one row per tag, so SUM(o.total) counts an order's total once per tag -> inflated revenue.

expected_observations.statement: The query is trying to total all order revenue.
The join to order_tags is one-to-many, duplicating each order's row per tag, so SUM(o.total) double/triple-counts.
Fix: sum from orders alone (no tag join), or aggregate tags in a separate subquery.
Inflation scales with tags per order (an order with 3 tags is counted 3x).
Correct result 10,000; this query returns 18,000.

decoys.why_it_looks_wrong: A scalar SUM with no GROUP BY can look like it's missing a grouping clause.
decoys.why_its_actually_fine: A single aggregate over the whole result set needs no GROUP BY — that is not the defect.

static_findings: aggregate over a one-to-many join without de-duplication

items.prompt: This query should list each customer with their number of orders, including customers with none. Explain what it actually returns.

files.content:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*)
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.name;

fault_label.description: With a LEFT JOIN, a customer with no orders still yields one NULL-padded row; COUNT(*) counts that row as 1 instead of 0. COUNT(o.id) counts non-null order ids -> 0.

expected_observations.statement: Intends to count orders per customer, keeping customers with zero orders.
COUNT(*) counts the single NULL-padded row a LEFT JOIN emits for an order-less customer, so they show 1 instead of 0.
Fix: COUNT(o.id) (any non-null column from the orders side).
The GROUP BY and LEFT JOIN are otherwise correct; only the COUNT argument is wrong.
Demonstrates the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) under NULLs.

decoys.why_it_looks_wrong: `GROUP BY c.name` could be flagged as unsafe if two customers share a name.
decoys.why_its_actually_fine: A reasonable robustness note, but not the bug under test; with the given data it groups correctly.

static_findings: COUNT(*) over LEFT JOIN result set

check.schema: CREATE TABLE customers(id INT, name TEXT);CREATE TABLE orders(id INT, customer_id INT);INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Ayesha'),(2,'Bilal'),(3,'Chaudhry');INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1),(11,1),(12,2);
check.correct: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id GROUP BY c.name

items.prompt: Read this function. Explain what it computes and whether it is correct.

files.content:
def sum_first_k(arr, k):
    total = 0
    i = 0
    while i < k - 1:
        total += arr[i]
        i += 1
    return total

fault_label.description: Loop runs while `i < k-1`, so it sums only the first k-1 elements instead of k.

expected_observations.statement: Means to sum the first k elements of arr.
`while i < k - 1` stops one short, summing k-1 elements, not k.
Fix: use `while i < k`.
Concrete case: sum_first_k([1,2,3,4,5], 3) returns 3, should be 6.
Complexity is O(k); the defect is correctness.

decoys.why_it_looks_wrong: Starting `total` at 0 could look like it mishandles empty input.
decoys.why_its_actually_fine: 0 is the correct identity for a sum; empty/zero-k returns 0 fine.
